transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-12-01 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Oliver (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO Celestia), Luca (Platform), Samir (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): Call was a deep discovery about latency and concurrency requirements; asked about p95 for streaming and token throughput; discussed private VPC and KMS; agreed on pilot.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from Redwood, gonna run through quickly what'd we like to cover, and then hand over to oliver for the deeper perf questions. you all good with that?
[00:12] Priya: yep thanks, we have about an hour, we want to make sure we get into p95 and how you handle streaming — we've got real-time chat agents so tail matters.
[00:23] Oliver: sweet, quick qualifier — what's your current stack? are you on k8s with Triton or is this serverless right now?
[00:30] Luca: currently k8s, custom inference plane, using a mix of on-prem gpus and cloud. we call a hosted vendor for prototyping but want predictable tail as we ramp.
[00:40] Samir: our SREs are worried about big spikes — we saw a token-flood last quarter and latency spiked to many seconds p95. so predictable p95 is top criterion.
[00:54] Oliver: ok, when you say p95 what number target do you have in mind? is it per-token or per-request?
[01:02] Priya: target is 200ms p95 for streaming responses (per-token), and sub-1s p95 for full request end-to-end for typical 150 token responses. if we had to pick one it's the streaming tail.
[01:15] Maya: got it. that maps to what other customers call low-200s per-token p95, which is tight but achievable with dedicated infra + KV/prefix caching depending on model.
[01:25] Oliver: quick note — streaming p95 is usually dominated by scheduling/batching latency for small tokens; if you use dedicated capacity we can give you reserved concurrency which removes cold scheduling jitter. also prefix cache helps if you have repeated prompts.
[01:38] Luca: what's the tradeoff on cost there? dedicated vs hosted — we care about cost but can't accept noisy tail.
[01:45] Maya: hosted gives fastest time to value, but if you need p95 predictability at scale, Dedicated pools are recommended. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives the most control for network and KMS but carries operational overhead.
[01:58] Samir: can we get the same p95 on hosted if we pay for a higher tier?
[02:03] Oliver: to a point — hosted has multi-tenant optimizations, and we do offer SLA tiers, but the absolute lowest jitter for heavy concurrency typically comes from dedicated. for example, customers running 800 concurrent streams with >100 tokens per stream saw p95 improve ~30% after moving to dedicated pools. that's anecdotal but we can reproduce.
[02:22] Priya: ok, about concurrency — we plan to run 600-1,200 concurrent user sessions during peak, average response length ~120 tokens, peak bursts up to 3k concurrent for short windows.
[02:34] Maya: that's helpful. two things we'll map: steady-state throughput (what sustained token/sec you need) and surge capacity (burst handling). what distribution do you have for tokens per request?
[02:44] Luca: median 90, 95th 250, some outliers up to 1k. so p95 of tokens is high.
[02:52] Oliver: ok so our benchmark matrix should include median and p95 token lengths. also measure both streaming per-token tail and end-to-end completion p95. we'll want to know observed token/sec, average tokens per second per GPU, and how batching/quantization affects tail.
[03:10] Samir: speak to quantization — we use a 8-bit quantized model on prem, any differences we should expect?
[03:16] Oliver: quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but can change latency profile slightly. for streaming, if quantization changes kernel choices, you may see different per-token perf; we'll include quantized variants in the test matrix.
[03:30] Priya: what about model fallbacks — if a big spike happens can you route to a cheaper model or reduce tokens?
[03:36] Maya: yep we have routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, region-first. automatic fallback to smaller model variants or cached completions is an option — we can set thresholds so that at 80% capacity we start tail mitigation.
[03:48] Luca: interested in KV cache — we do a lot of multi-turn chat, reuse is high. does Redwood do kv cache across requests?
[03:55] Oliver: yes, continuous KV cache for multi-turn is supported in our runtime; on dedicated you can keep warm KV across sessions which helps p95 a lot. on hosted, we do per-request caching where feasible but dedicated gives you stronger guarantees.
[04:08] Priya: security — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs for egress. can you do HSM?
[04:18] Maya: SOC2 report is available; SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported; for KMS we integrate with cloud KMS and can support bring-your-own-key via HSM in Private deployments. we'll attach the security pack.
[04:32] Samir: network-wise for private we'd want VPC peering and control plane in our network, is that possible?
[04:38] Oliver: yes for Private deployments we do VPC-and on-prem options, private control plane, we can lock down egress, and provide audit logs for each token request. there is some deployment lead time.
[04:52] Maya: quick note on benchmarks — important knobs: sequence length, batching window, concurrency, model variant, quantization. we'll test p50/p95/p99 for streaming token latency and p95 for end-to-end.
[05:06] Priya: how do you measure streaming latency — at token emit or after network serialization? we need end-to-end numbers including our frontend websocket overhead.
[05:15] Oliver: we'll measure both: raw server-side token emit (time between server step completions) and end-to-end measured from request start to first token emitted and to completion; we'll also capture network RTT so you can add your websocket overhead.
[05:28] Luca: can we run the benchmarks against our trace? we can mask customer data but want the same distribution.
[05:34] Maya: yes, please send a 2-week trace of request lengths and arrival times. we'll replay at scaled rates for the pilot.
[05:43] Priya: what about throttling rules and graceful degradation? need a plan so we don't return 500s during spikes.
[05:50] Oliver: Redwood has throttling tiers and graceful fallback policies — e.g., if queue > threshold, route to smaller model, or return cached short answers. we can also queue with priority. we'll show sample configs.
[06:05] Samir: curious about token/sec numbers per GPU. can you give ballpark for gpt-style decoder throughput?
[06:12] Oliver: ballpark depends on model size and quantization. for a 7B open decoder quantized to 4/8-bit on modern A100-like instance you might expect ~5k-15k tokens/sec per GPU in inference mode; for larger 30B models maybe 1k-4k tokens/sec. but streaming tail is more sensitive to scheduler jitter than raw tokens/sec.
[06:35] Priya: given our load (1k concurrent, avg 120 tokens), what should we expect for capacity?
[06:42] Oliver: rough calc: 1k concurrent * 120 tokens = 120k tokens in flight, divided by say 5k tokens/sec per GPU -> ~24 GPUs sustained; add headroom for burst and autoscale and recommend starting with 30-36 GPUs in dedicated reserved pool for steady state and burst policies. we'll refine after seeing your trace.
[07:05] Luca: nice, can you include cost estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted for that footprint?
[07:10] Maya: yes we'll provide a pricing estimate in the follow-up; dedicated has lower per-token cost at scale but upfront commit. hosted is more elastic but a bit higher unit cost.
[07:22] Priya: any SLAs on p95? we need contractual p95 of 500ms for streaming or we won't consider hosted.
[07:30] Maya: we have tiers; hosted default SLA is network+service availability, but we can discuss a dedicated SLA that includes latency SLOs for reserved capacity — we'll need to scope exact SLOs in the contract.
[07:44] Samir: what's deployment time for Private? we're regulated and may need everything on prem or in our VPC.
[07:51] Oliver: Private deployments typically take 6-10 weeks depending on connectivity and HSM setup. there are appliance options for air-gapped envs as well.
[07:59] Priya: ok good to know. next, how do you instrument and expose per-token cost/latency? our finance team needs per-route token cost breakdowns.
[08:10] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdown, per-route dashboards and tracing hooks; we'll give you example screenshots.
[08:20] Luca: we also want to test failover — if a region loses capacity, can you fail to another region without user-visible spike?
[08:27] Oliver: yes, smart routing with automated fallback to compatible model variants in other regions is supported; there can be a small ramp in latency during failover but we can configure fanout/priming to reduce visible impact.
[08:40] Priya: let's talk pilot specifics — we want a 2-week pilot that replays our trace at 1x and 2x, measures streaming p95, end-to-end p95, tokens/sec, and error rates.
[08:51] Maya: agreed. pilot plan: week 0 (prep) — share trace and prompts, week 1 — run 1x replay on hosted and on dedicated small pool, week 2 — 2x replay and run quantized variant. deliverables: benchmark report, configs, and cost estimate.
[09:05] Samir: timeline ok, who'll own the pilot kickoff?
[09:08] Priya: i'll own internal signoff and give the trace.
[09:12] Maya: perfect — we'll schedule kickoff for 2026-12-08 15:00 UTC, send calendar invite after.
[09:18] (small cross talk)
[09:24] Oliver: one more technical note: streaming p95 often improves significantly if you tune batching windows: aggressive batching improves tokens/sec but can hurt per-token latency; we'll test multiple batching profiles.
[09:39] Luca: are there tooling APIs to dynamically change batching or route policies?
[09:43] Maya: yes we expose APIs and console toggles for routing and batching profiles; we can automate rollouts.
[09:50] Priya: any red flags we've seen in other engagements?
[09:54] Oliver: typical surprises: token distribution tail bigger than expected, leading to underprovision; also client-side websocket timeouts cutting off long responses; and misspecified caching keys that prevent reuse. we'll checklist those in the pilot prep doc.
[10:10] Priya: ok great. can you also add a test for cold-start latency vs warm? we saw big variance on cold starts.
[10:16] Oliver: yes we'll include cold vs warm scenarios and kv-cache warmup.
[10:22] Maya: quick recap of next steps: we'll send bench template, security pack, and pricing; schedule pilot kickoff 12/08; you send trace and prompts by 12/04.
[10:33] Priya: i'll get that to you, and loop in compliance.
[10:36] Maya: thanks everyone, any other questions?
[10:39] Samir: none here.
[10:41] Priya: all set.
[10:43] Maya: great, we'll follow up in email with attachments. thanks!

(Transcript ends - auto timestamps approximate)
